extracted.intended_audience: citizens, political philosophers, and readers concerned with the legitimacy of resistance and government dissolution
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and standards for when a government is legitimately dissolved and when the people may resist or establish a new legislative. Covers causes (e.g., alteration of elections, foreign subjection, failure to execute laws, breach of trust), limits on resistance, who judges, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alteration of electors or ways of election without consent
rubrics_metrics.description: When, by the arbitrary power of the prince, the electors, or ways of election, are altered, without the consent, and contrary to the common interest of the people, there also the legislative is altered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If those chosen are not the legislative appointed by the people (because electors or election methods were changed), the legislative is effectively altered and government dissolved (Sect. 216).

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery of the people into subjection to a foreign power
rubrics_metrics.description: The delivery also of the people into the subjection of a foreign power, either by the prince, or by the legislative, is certainly a change of the legislative, and so a dissolution of the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Loss of independent governance to a foreign power defeats the end of society (being preserved as an independent body), and thus dissolves the government (Sect. 217).

rubrics_metrics.name: Neglect or abandonment of executive so laws cannot be executed
rubrics_metrics.description: When he who has the supreme executive power neglects and abandons that charge, so that the laws already made can no longer be put in execution, this is demonstratively to reduce all to anarchy, and so effectually to dissolve the government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A government where laws cannot be executed is equivalent to no government; absence of administration of justice and public direction removes the bonds of society (Sect. 219).

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative or prince acting contrary to their trust (invading property)
rubrics_metrics.description: The legislative acts against the trust reposed in them, when they endeavour to invade the property of the subject, and to make themselves, or any part of the community, masters, or arbitrary disposers of the lives, liberties, or fortunes of the people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When legislators or the supreme executor seek to destroy property or reduce people to slavery, they forfeit their authority and put themselves into a state of war with the people, who are absolved from obedience and may establish a new legislative (Sects. 221–222).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corrupting or preengaging electors/representatives
rubrics_metrics.description: When the prince employs the force, treasure and offices of the society to corrupt the representatives, and gain them to his purposes; or openly preengages the electors, and prescribes to their choice, such whom he has by sollicitations, threats, promises, or otherwise, won to his designs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regulating candidates and electors in this way cuts up government by the roots and poisons public security; preparation of a compliant assembly is a breach of trust tantamount to subverting government (Sect. 222).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to erect a new legislative to prevent or cure oppression
rubrics_metrics.description: When the government is dissolved the people are at liberty to provide for themselves, by erecting a new legislative, differing from the other, by the change of persons, or form, or both, as they shall find it most for their safety and good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This right exists not only after oppression but as a preventive remedy—people may act to prevent tyranny before it becomes incurable; waiting until chains are on is mockery (Sect. 220).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance limited to defence, not revenge or punishment of superior
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-defence is a part of the law of nature; the community may resist injury even against the king, but they must only defend themselves and not attack their prince or exceed bounds of due reverence and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance may repel present attempts but must not seek retribution for past violences or punish a superior as such; the aim is defense and preservation, not revenge (Sects. 233–235).

rubrics_metrics.name: Intent or design to destroy the commonwealth as ground for resistance
rubrics_metrics.description: If a king has a purpose and design to ruin the kingdom and commonwealth (examples: Nero, Caligula), he immediately gives up all care of the commonwealth and forfeits the power of governing his subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A ruler who seriously promotes the destruction of the commonwealth ‘dethrones himself’ and ceases to be a king, making resistance lawful (Sects. 237–239).

rubrics_metrics.name: Making the kingdom dependent on another (alienation of the realm)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a king makes himself the dependent of another, and subjects his kingdom (alienation of the kingdom) to another's dominion, he loses the principal part of regal dignity and thereby forfeits his authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if not intended to harm the people, alienation of the kingdom's independence constitutes loss of royal authority and frees the people to act (Sect. 238).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of force without right creates a state of war and cancels former ties
rubrics_metrics.description: Whosoever uses force without right... puts himself into a state of war with those against whom he so uses it; and in that state all former ties are cancelled... every one has a right to defend himself, and to resist the aggressor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle applies against magistrates as well as foreigners—using force without law places the actor outside the lawful order and justifies defensive resistance (Sects. 231–232).

rubrics_metrics.name: Those who by force remove or subvert the legislative are rebels
rubrics_metrics.description: If any one by force takes away the established legislative of any society, and the laws by them made... he thereby takes away the umpirage... They, who remove, or change the legislative, take away this decisive power... and so destroying the authority... they actually introduce a state of war.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both usurpers who remove the legislative and legislators who invade the ends of their trust (making themselves arbitrary) are guilty of rebellion; the people may treat them accordingly (Sect. 227).

rubrics_metrics.name: Revolutions arise from long trains of abuses, not mere mismanagement
rubrics_metrics.description: Great mistakes, many wrong and inconvenient laws, and the slips of human frailty, will be borne by the people; but if a long train of abuses, prevarications and artifices, all tending the same way, make the design visible to the people, they may rise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Revolution is not a response to occasional errors; it is justified when abuses are persistent, pervasive, and clearly indicate a design against the people's liberties (Sect. 225).

rubrics_metrics.name: Who shall judge whether the prince or legislative act contrary to trust
rubrics_metrics.description: The people shall be judge; who so proper to judge as the body of the people (who lodged that trust), to determine how far the trust was meant to extend?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the prince or administration declines public determination, the appeal lies to heaven—individuals must judge for themselves when no earthly umpire exists (Sects. 240–242).

rubrics_metrics.name: People may prevent evil by resisting designs before they are executed
rubrics_metrics.description: The mischief which is designed them, the people may prevent before it be done: such designs when any king harbours in his thoughts and seriously promotes, he immediately gives up all care of the commonwealth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allowance for preemptive resistance: intentional designs toward tyranny can be taken as sufficient cause for resistance before the mischief is complete (Sect. 239 and commentary on Barclay).
